fixes.explanation: Mordecai, who raised Esther (Esther 2:7), tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1). In this chapter, that's what mourning looks like (Esther 4:3). He doesn't keep it quiet, either, because he goes out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly. His clothes and his voice say the same thing, friend.

Haman is the king's top official (Esther 3:1), and the text never sends Mordecai to his door. Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and goes out into the middle of the city (Esther 4:1). I think knocking on Haman's door would be a very short conversation anyway. Mordecai takes his grief out into the city instead.

The text gives no instruction from Esther here. Her maidens and eunuchs come and tell her about Mordecai in the next verses (Esther 4:4). The reason he stops is the law: no one wearing sackcloth could enter the king's gate (Esther 4:2). Mordecai just walked as far as the rules would let him.

Esther 4:3 says that in every province to which the king's command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. "They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes." Fasting means going without food, and it's part of how they mourn. News about the decree travels far, and so does the grief. It's a sad picture, friend, and I think we should let it be sad.

Fleeing isn't what the verse describes, friend. Esther 4:3 says that in every province to which the king's command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes. The word that fits is fasted.

Esther 4:4 says that when her maidens and eunuchs told her about Mordecai, the queen was overcome with distress. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. Her first move is to get him something else to wear, and that's a caring thing to do, friend. I think she wanted to help however she could.

There's no silver in this verse. Esther 4:4 says the queen was overcome with distress and sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. Her gift answers his sackcloth directly. It has nothing to do with getting him out of the city.

Not in this verse, friend. Esther 4:4 says the queen was overcome with distress and sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. Her gift is aimed at the sackcloth itself. Nothing in the verse tells him to go home.
Not quite, friend. Esther 4:4 says she sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, "…but he would not accept them." Mordecai turns the clothes down. That's a no from him.
That's right. Esther sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, but he would not accept them (Esther 4:4). Mordecai turns the clothes down. Her gift gets a no.

Yes, friend. Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to her. She sent him to Mordecai "…to learn what was troubling him and why." (Esther 4:5). So she sends someone to go find out what's troubling him. Hathach is about to get a lot of steps in.

Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach all that had happened, including "…the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews." Haman is the king's top official (Esther 3:1). Mordecai passes along the exact figure. That's a very specific detail, friend.

The text doesn't mention soldiers in this detail. Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach all that had happened, including the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews. So the number in this verse is a sum promised to the treasury, not a headcount of anyone. Haman, the king's top official (Esther 3:1), is the one who promised it.

No helpers are named in this verse. Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach all that had happened to him, including the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews. The one making that promise is Haman, the king's top official (Esther 3:1). Nobody else is listed beside him.

Esther 4:8 says Mordecai gave Hathach "…a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews…" to show and explain to Esther. So she gets to see the decree itself, not just hear about it. Hathach carries it to her and explains it. That's a lot to put in someone's hands, friend.

The ring was used to seal the decree (Esther 3:12), but it isn't what Mordecai hands over. Esther 4:8 says he gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa. Hathach was to show and explain it to Esther. What Mordecai sends is the decree, not the ring.

The text doesn't have a letter from Haman. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews. Hathach was to show and explain it to Esther. So what she's shown is the decree about her own people.

It's true, actually. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai urged her "…to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people." That's three requests packed into one verse. And he sends the decree along with it.

Titles aren't what the law mentions. Esther 4:11 says the person who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned is to be put to death. Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live. Losing titles isn't part of what she describes.

Mordecai says, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) Esther is living inside the palace. Mordecai tells her not to imagine that being there means she alone will escape. That's a tough thing to hear, friend.

Mordecai says that if she remains silent, relief for the Jews will arise from another place, "…but you and your father’s house will perish." (Esther 4:14) Perish is a strong word. I think Mordecai wants her to hear how serious this is. There's no sprinkles on that sentence, friend.

Hiding isn't in Mordecai's warning, friend. He says that if Esther remains silent, "…you and your father’s house will perish." (Esther 4:14) Just before that, he tells her not to imagine that being in the palace means she alone will escape (Esther 4:13). The word is perish.

Mordecai doesn't say that. He asks, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) He leaves it as an open question about this time. Nothing in it says she was never meant to be queen.

Scribes aren't mentioned in her plan. Esther says, "…I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) Her maidens join her in the fast, and she asks Mordecai to gather the Jews who can be found in Susa to fast for her. Maidens is the word for the blank, friend.

The officials aren't in this verse. Esther says, "…I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) So the fast has two groups: the Jews who can be found in Susa, and Esther with her maidens. Maidens fills the blank.

Yes, friend. Esther says, "After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law." (Esther 4:16) First comes the fast, and after that she says she will go. She knows what the law says about going uninvited (Esther 4:11), and she says it anyway.

It's true, actually. Esther says, "After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law." (Esther 4:16) She has already told Mordecai about the law (Esther 4:11). So she makes this promise knowing exactly what the law says.
